---
title: "Research Themes"
description: "Research on primordial black hole evaporation, early-universe cosmology, and the dark matter abundance of black hole remnants."
toc: true
---

I study how light primordial black holes (PBHs) change the evolution of the early universe. If they are abundant enough, they can briefly dominate the energy density before they evaporate. I model this transition to work out how much radiation the evaporation produces and how much dark matter any surviving remnants could account for.

## Planck-scale remnants from loop quantum gravity

In the scenario we consider, motivated by loop quantum gravity, Hawking evaporation ends with a long-lived remnant of approximately the Planck mass. We calculate which initial PBH masses and abundances are compatible with the observed radiation and dark matter densities. In this model, a population with initial masses near one tonne can reheat the early universe and leave enough remnants to make up the observed dark matter.

## Memory burden and massive remnants

Memory-burden models propose that information stored in a black hole can slow its evaporation. I study scenarios in which this suppression becomes important after the black hole has lost about half its initial mass. The surviving objects can then be much heavier than the Planck mass. I use cosmological constraints to investigate which initial masses and abundances could give a viable population of such remnants.
